pages.title: Blockade of the Gaza Strip
pages.extract:
The blockade of the Gaza Strip is an ongoing land, air, and sea blockade imposed by Israel regulating the movement of people and goods into and out of the Gaza Strip. Exit and entry into Gaza by sea or air is prohibited, and Israel controls two of Gaza's three border crossings, while Egypt controls the Rafah crossing on Gaza's southern border. Israel's stated aims are to prevent the smuggling of weapons and dual-use materials into Gaza, halt rocket attacks, and exert economic and political pressure on Hamas.
Israeli restrictions on movement and goods in the Gaza Strip date to the early 1990s, during its military occupation of the Gaza Strip (1967–2005), with intermittent blockades in 2005–2006. In June 2007, after Hamas seized control of the Gaza Strip, Israel significantly intensified existing restrictions and imposed an indefinite blockade that remains in place, citing the departure of Fatah and Palestinian Authority security forces, the need to hold Hamas accountable for rocket attacks on Israeli territory, and the aim of constraining its ability to govern Gaza. In the same year, Egypt closed the Rafah border crossing. Israel further tightened the blockade following the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.
Israel regulates Palestinians' movement through the Erez Crossing, with applications considered only for merchants, workers, and limited medical and humanitarian reasons. Before the Gaza war, exits via Erez averaged about 40,000 monthly. Imports are heavily restricted, with "dual use" items (including construction material and computer equipment) permitted only as part of donor projects. Israel's ban on virtually all exports from the Strip remains the main impediment to Gaza's sustainable economic development. Israel has also been accused of failing to fulfill obligations under various ceasefire agreements to ease or lift the blockade.
While the blockade's legality has not been adjudicated in court, human rights groups, international community representatives, and legal professionals have decried it as a form of collective punishment in contravention of international law, specifically the Fourth Geneva Convention, as it restricts the flow of essential goods, contributes to economic hardship, and limits Gazans' freedom of movement. Rights groups have held Israel mainly responsible as the occupying power. The land, sea, and air blockade isolated Gaza from the rest of the occupied Palestinian territory and the world, leading to the territory being called an "open-air prison".
